title: Self-care among people with heart failure in Uganda: Challenges and potential solutions
content:
by Dorah Nampijja, Elias Kumbakumba, Julian Adong, Stephen Asiimwe, Jessica E. Haberer

Heart failure (HF) accounts for up to 43% of all hospital admissions among adults globally and has a high one-year mortality of up to 8%. Although no African guidelines currently advise on HF self -care management, the European Society of Cardiology recommends that all HF patients receive education and support to facilitate self-care. Self-care among HF has been reported to improve health outcomes, reduce morbidity and mortality. This paper aims to evaluate the barriers and perceived solutions associated with self-care among HF patients in Uganda. We undertook an exploratory qualitative study that was grounded in the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) through which we explored barriers and their solutions to self-care for HF patients. We carried out 10 in-depth interviews consisting of 5 health workers who manage HF and 5 HF patients post hospitalization, and one additional focus group discussion involving 6HF patients. Barriers to self-care were categorized into themes according to TPB. Participants expressed negative attitudes towards HF self-care, which included difficulty in initiating and sustaining self-care, lack of self -discipline, and lack of motivation due to slow resolution of symptoms. As subjective norms, participants described how limited health workers support, inadequate social support and negative peer pressure served as barriers to HF self-care. Lack of understanding of the importance of self-care and lack of finances were the identified barriers as perceived limits to behavioral control. Solutions to HF self-care barriers included education about self-care, availability of affordable and sustainable medicines, and improved social support. Practicing self-care among people with HF is challenging and there it is essential to support the uptake of self-care to ensure better health outcomes.
